children: By Amanda Cooper
Euro zone bond yields broadly fell on Tuesday, with French sovereign bond yields stabilising, as oil prices moved lower on renewed market attention to possible progress for Middle East peace talks.

French 10-year OAT yields (FR10YT=RR), which fell around 11 basis points on Monday after avoiding a downgrade last Friday from ratings agency Moody's, were last steady at 4.91%. They had risen earlier in the day as investors took profits on the largest daily fall in five months the day before.

Official French data showed consumer morale in the euro zone's second-largest economy fell to its lowest since 2013 in early October, when protests were building towards the worst civil unrest in years.
French student leaders vowed on Monday to go on protesting despite concessions on education from President Emmanuel Macron's government.

"We see little prospect of an immediate political settlement or budget agreement. With parliamentary proceedings set to continue for several weeks, French fiscal policy is likely to remain a source of market tension," said Anthony Willis, a senior economist at Columbia Threadneedle.
Oil, meanwhile, extended its dip and was last down 1.7% on the day at $113.85 a barrel

as attention turned to Middle East peace efforts. Prices, however, remain near multi-month highs as the Houthi-Saudi Arabia conflict rages and the potential for fresh US-Israeli attacks on Iran hangs over the market.
European natural gas prices (TFMBMc1) also eased on the day, but stayed close to four-year highs on the back of tight supply and colder weather across the region.

Against that backdrop, the yield on German 10-year Bunds (DE10YT=RR), a safe-haven asset that acts as a benchmark for the wider euro zone bond market, was down 1.1 bps on the day at 3.34%, while 2-year Schatz yields (DE2YT=RR) fell 4.3 bps to 3.036%.
BELGIAN BONDS UNDER PRESSURE

Swaps that reflect expectations for euro zone consumer inflation in a year's time (EUCPIZ1Y=TWEB) are not far off 4%, double the European Central Bank's target rate and just shy of April's three-year high of 3.987%, according to LSEG data.
Market-based measures of inflation expectations have been grinding higher as the
has dragged on.

With concern intensifying over the ability of the euro zone's more indebted members to tackle their debt piles as borrowing costs rise, investors are turning increasingly to the bonds of those countries with better finances, such as Germany.

The German debt agency sold some €3.8 billion in a top-up of a 2-year Schatz on Tuesday for an average yield of 3.08%, down from an average yield of 3.1% at the last 2-year sale in late September. Demand also improved, according to the bid-to-cover ratio, which rose to 1.3, from 1.1 at the last sale of this maturity.
Belgian bonds have also been in the line of fire recently, given the country's high debt burden.
Belgian yields (BE10YT=RR), which on Tuesday were up just over 1 bp at 4.4%, have risen this month, although far more modestly than French yields.

Belgium sold some €1.3 billion in 10-year debt on Monday, for an average yield of 4.41% and a bid-to-cover ratio of 1.63, compared with an average yield of 4.299% and a bid-to-cover of 1.72 at the last 10-year auction in September.

The European Central Bank delivers its decision on interest rates on Thursday and is widely expected to leave monetary policy unchanged. But, with money markets currently pricing in a high chance of a hike in December and fully pricing in a second by April, investors will be focused on any hints from President Christine Lagarde on the likelihood of these outcomes (0#EURIRPR).
